steps.title: Yes, it is farther
steps.say: You are right: in early July, Earth is actually a little farther from the Sun than in January.

ops.text: Early July: Earth is slightly farther from the Sun.

steps.title: Distance is too small to matter
steps.say: But the distance change is only about three percent. That is much too small to explain winter and summer.

ops.text: Distance change: only ~3% — far too small to make summer.

steps.title: The tilt changes sunlight
steps.say: What really matters is the tilt. It changes how high the Sun gets in the sky and how long daylight lasts.

ops.text: • how high the Sun climbs in the sky
• how many hours of daylight there are

steps.title: Summer: high Sun, long days
steps.say: In northern summer, the northern half of Earth is tilted toward the Sun. The Sun is high and daylight is long, so it gets hot.

ops.text: Northern summer: high Sun + long daylight = more heat.

steps.title: Winter: low Sun, short days
steps.say: In northern winter, the northern half is tilted away from the Sun. The Sun stays low and daylight is short, so it stays cold.

ops.text: Northern winter: low Sun + short daylight = less heat.

steps.title: It is about angle, not distance
steps.say: So summer is not hot because Earth is closer. It is hot because the tilted hemisphere receives sunlight more directly for more hours.

ops.text: Seasons come from the tilt, not from distance.
